name: Vignola's Composite Order

authority.source: Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura, Rome 1562, plates XXVI-XXVIII
authority.author: Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola
authority.note: Vignola counts the Composite, with the Tuscan, as one of the two Italian orders against the three Greek. His entablature is drawn from Roman examples; the Arch of Titus is the ancient case Esquie sets beside it.

module.name: Semidiameter of the column at the base of the shaft
module.note: Eighteen parts, as for the Ionic and Corinthian.

fluting.profile: semicircular flutes separated by fillets, the fillets two sevenths the width of the flutes

members.name: Plinth of the pedestal base
members.note: Esquie: 'the plinth of its base may be increased from 4 parts to 8 parts' - Vignola's drawn figure is 4, the enlargement is offered as a licence.

members.name: Cyma recta of the pedestal base
Die (dado)
members.note: The die is two squares high: 100 parts high by 50 parts wide (Vignola 1889 plate XX; Esquie plate XXIX). Half-width 25 parts, on which the column base at half-width 25 sits exactly.

members.name: Cyma reversa of the pedestal cap
Plinth
members.note: One third of the base, 1/6 D (Ware). Half-width 25 parts = 18 + Vignola's stated 7 parts of projection, which is also the half-width of the pedestal die.

members.name: Fillet at the foot of the shaft
Shaft proper
members.note: 16 modules 12 parts including the fillets and astragal (Vignola 1889, plate XXIII). 24 semicircular flutes separated by fillets, the flutes sometimes cabled to a third of their height. Diminution 5/6, beginning at one third of the shaft height.

members.name: First (lower) row of eight acanthus leaves
members.note: Vignola makes the two rows of leaves of the same dimensions as the Corinthian, but changes them from olive to acanthus (Vignola 1889, plate XXVII).

members.name: Second (upper) row of eight acanthus leaves
Ionic volutes with the echinus between them
members.note: Vignola 1889: 'This volute is, with the abacus, 16 parts high.' The abacus is 6, so the volute zone is 10. The egg-and-dart echinus that makes the bell prominent occupies the SAME 10 parts, standing between and behind the volutes - it is not stacked above or below them, which is why it is not a separate member here. The volutes are set out exactly as the Ionic (Esquie plate XXIII), four of them, diagonally, as in Scamozzi's angular capital; in place of the Corinthian's small central helices the Composite puts two flowers.

members.name: Ovolo of the abacus
members.note: Plan and profile of the abacus as the Corinthian, with a flower in the centre of each side.

members.name: First fascia
members.note: LOW CONFIDENCE. Vignola's Composite architrave is drawn on plate XXVIII of the Regola and its member figures are not transcribed in the 1889 translation, in Esquie, or in Ware, all of which say only that the Composite entablature repeats the Corinthian proportions with 'fewer and larger' details and without the modillions. Two fascias rather than the Corinthian's three are encoded on that authority; a three-fascia reading is defensible and the 27-part total is not in doubt either way.

members.name: Frieze
members.enrichment: richly carved foliate scroll in the Roman examples Vignola drew from

members.name: Astragal at the top of the frieze
Cyma reversa of the bed mould
Dentil band
members.note: The Composite dentil is the large one: 1/5 D high (7.2 parts), 1/6 D wide (6 parts), interdentil 1/12 D (3 parts), therefore 1/4 D = 9 parts on centres - half again the Ionic and Corinthian dentil (Ware). Because there are no modillions, Esquie notes the dentils 'may be set out regardless of the axes of the columns', which is the single greatest practical licence in the five orders.

members.name: Crowning fillet
members.note: Projection taken at 36 parts on Ware's general rule that the cornice projects as much as it is high; Vignola's own figure for the Composite cornice projection is not transcribed in the sources consulted, whereas his Ionic (31) and Corinthian (38) are.

invariants.statement: The entablature is one quarter the height of the column, base and capital included.
The pedestal is 7 modules, 0.35 of the column - the Corinthian pedestal, and like it an exception to Vignola's general one-third rule.
invariants.note: Vignola: 'The Composite Pedestal is like the Corinthian, with exception of a few details.' Esquie: the pedestal and base 'differ from the Corinthian Order only in the mouldings of the pedestal.' Neither source restates the height, so it is inherited; medium confidence attaches to the inheritance, not to the arithmetic.

invariants.statement: The column is 20 modules, that is ten diameters - the Corinthian column exactly.
Base, shaft and capital make the column.
Architrave, frieze and cornice make the entablature.
The capital is one diameter and one sixth, as the Corinthian: the plan and profile have the same proportions.
The volute with the abacus is 16 parts, which is 8/21 of the capital.
The upper diameter is five sixths of the lower.
The shaft is cylindrical for its lower third and diminishes above.

named_spacings.name: pycnostyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian, not Vignola's. Vignola gives no named series; the names are carried here because American practice reads them onto him. Ware's American Vignola simplifies the series to 1, 2, 3 and 4 diameters clear.

named_spacings.name: eustyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian. This is the one Vignola's own Ionic colonnade lands on exactly.

named_spacings.name: araeostyle
named_spacings.note: Vitruvian; requires a timber architrave. Ware notes the ancients spaced Tuscan columns with wooden architraves as much as seven diameters apart.

named_spacings.name: vignola-composite-colonnade
named_spacings.note: Inherited from the Corinthian: axes 6 2/3 modules, 2 1/3 diameters clear. But the reason for that figure does not survive the inheritance. In the Corinthian it exists so that a modillion falls on every axis; the Composite cornice has no modillions, and Esquie says the dentils 'may be set out regardless of the axes of the columns'. The Composite is therefore the one rich order whose bay is free.

named_spacings.name: vignola-composite-arcade
named_spacings.note: As the Corinthian arcade: piers 3 modules, opening 9 by 18, axes 12 modules.

named_spacings.name: vignola-composite-arcade-on-pedestals
named_spacings.note: As the Corinthian: axes 16 modules, 32 parts to the whole - 7 pedestal, 20 column, 5 entablature, with the same deliberate departure from the 2:1 arch.

derived_rules.note: A quarter of the column, at any scale. The Composite carries the Corinthian's weight without the Corinthian's modillion discipline, which is exactly why it was the order of choice for triumphal arches and for anything whose bay was set by something other than the cornice.
derived_rules.authority_note: Vignola, Regola; Esquie plate XXXIV: the proportions of this order are those of the Corinthian.

derived_rules.note: The cornice member of the entablature, 4 of 10 parts. Same figure as the Corinthian; the difference is what is in it - dentils at 1/4 diameter on centres instead of modillions.

Projection equal to height, on Ware's general rule. Vignola's own figure for the Composite cornice projection is not in any transcription consulted, unlike the Ionic (31 parts) and the Corinthian (2 modules 2 parts); this is the weakest number in the pack.
derived_rules.authority_note: Ware's general rule, not Vignola's drawn figure. Treat as provisional.

derived_rules.note: The Composite dentil is the big one: 1/6 D wide (6 parts) with a 1/12 D interdentil (3 parts), so 1/4 D = 9 parts on centres, and 1/5 D high. Half again the Ionic and Corinthian dentil. At the default 6 in module that is a 3 in spacing with a 2 in dentil - the only dentil in the five orders that is comfortable to run in stock millwork.

Because there are no modillions and the dentils are large, the Composite dentil course need not resolve to the column axis. This is a real licence and the only one of its kind in the rich orders; it is why the Composite survives contemporary bay-setting when the Corinthian does not.
derived_rules.authority_note: Esquie, plate XXXVIII: 'as the dentils are relatively small, they may be set out regardless of the axes of the columns.'

derived_rules.note: Of ceiling_height. As the Corinthian: the room is heavy above and needs weight below.

Of the floor-to-cornice height. The cap of the pedestal at room scale, 7 of the 32 modules of the whole order - about 26 in at a 10 ft ceiling. Furniture wants 32 to 36. Choose, and record the choice.

Of the floor-to-cornice height. The wainscot is the pedestal; Vignola shows the Composite pedestal mouldings unenriched, 'but they are often enriched' (Esquie), which makes this the pedestal to carve if anything is to be carved.

Of opening_width, on the architrave. LOW CONFIDENCE on the internal division: two fascias are encoded here on the strength of Ware's 'fewer and larger' details, but Vignola's plate XXVIII is not transcribed anywhere consulted and three fascias is a defensible reading.
Opening twice as high as wide, entablature a quarter of the door height.
Of opening_width. Retargeted at ontology 0.3.0: 'window_surround' was split by trade, and this rule belongs to window_surround_wood. The other heir needs its own rule and does not yet have one.

Envelope cornice. On a 12 ft storey, 14.4 in deep with a dentil course of 2 in dentils at 3 in on centres - a course that can be run in stock and mitred by a competent carpenter, which the Corinthian modillion course cannot.
Envelope frieze, 3 of 10. Vignola's Composite frieze is the one he expected to be richly carved; left plain it will look underfed against the cornice above it.

Where the Composite is used over another order - the standard superimposition, as at the Arch of Titus and in every Renaissance cortile - the belt at the storey line should read as the pedestal plinth of the order above, not as an applied band. Half a module is the minimum that will do that.

conflicts.statement: Almost no North American manufacturer stocks a true Vignola Composite capital. What is sold as 'Composite' is usually a Corinthian bell with four generic scrolls stuck on, missing the astragal and the egg-and-dart echinus that Vignola specifically adds to make the bell prominent, and with the volutes drawn as arcs rather than as true Ionic spirals.
conflicts.resolution: Specify by construction, not by name: two rows of eight acanthus leaves of Corinthian dimension; an astragal and an enriched egg-and-dart ovolo above them; four Ionic volutes set diagonally, drawn by Vignola's twelve-centre method with three turns, occupying 10 parts with the abacus above making 16; flowers in place of the Corinthian's central helices; a flower in each face of the abacus. If the maker cannot answer to that, buy a Corinthian and be honest about it.

conflicts.statement: The Composite capital is not cheaper than the Corinthian - the two lower rows of leaves are identical - but it reads richer from below because the volutes carry at distance where acanthus does not. Cost per unit of apparent richness is the best in the five orders.
conflicts.resolution: Where budget forces a choice between a good Composite and a compromised Corinthian, take the Composite. A well-made Composite is a better building than a Corinthian with one tier of leaves. And where the whole capital must be cast, the Composite casts better: the volute is a solid form that survives a mould, and deep-cut acanthus is what moulds lose first.

conflicts.statement: The fillets in this pack's Composite cornice run to 0.5 parts - 1/6 in at a 6 in module - and the corona and cymatium figures are reconstructions rather than transcriptions. Building small compounds an already soft number.
conflicts.resolution: Do not use this order below a 9 in module. Above it, hold 1/2 in minimum on every fillet and take the difference out of the corona, which is the member whose exact height is least load-bearing. And note in the submittal that the corona and cymatium split here is low confidence: if you have access to a good facsimile of Regola plate XXVIII, measure it and correct this pack.

conflicts.statement: The Composite's home is superimposition - Ionic or Corinthian below, Composite above, as in every Renaissance cortile and the Arch of Titus. Contemporary height limits and floor-area rules usually leave enough height for one order and not two, and the second storey is where the order gets cut.
conflicts.resolution: If only one order will fit, use one order. A Composite alone is perfectly correct. What does not work is starting a superimposition and abandoning it - a full lower order carrying a half-height upper one reads as a building that ran out of money, which it did. Where two orders do fit, Vignola's own rule applies: the upper diameter of the lower order becomes the lower diameter of the upper, so the upper order is shorter, and where two orders stand side by side the smaller is given two thirds the height of the larger.

sources: Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura, Rome 1562
Vignola, The Five Orders of Architecture, tr. Tommaso Juglaris & Warren Locke, Norwood Press 1889 (archive.org/details/fiveordersofarch00vign) - plates XIII-XXVIII
Pierre Esquie, The Five Orders of Architecture according to Vignola, 1930 (archive.org/details/pierreesuie) - plates XVIII-XXXIX
William R. Ware, The American Vignola, part I: The Five Orders, 1902/1920 (archive.org/details/americanvignola01wareuoft; en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Ware_-_The_American_Vignola,_1920.djvu)
Robert Chitham, The Classical Orders of Architecture, 2nd ed. 2005 - used for cross-check of member-level figures where the period plates carry the dimension only as a drawn annotation
theclassicalorders.com (Martin Brandwein / M. Gunnison Collins), Ionic and Corinthian layout sheets - cross-check only
notes:
THE ORDER MOST OFTEN DRAWN WRONG, SO SAY PLAINLY WHAT IT INHERITS.

FROM THE CORINTHIAN it takes: the column of 20 modules (ten diameters); the entablature of 5 modules, one quarter of the column, divided 3 : 3 : 4; the pedestal of 7 modules, including that pedestal's status as an exception to Vignola's own one-third rule; the base and the shaft entire, 1 module and 16 modules 12 parts, with 24 flutes; the capital's overall height of 2 modules 6 parts and its plan, a hollow-sided square on a 4-module diagonal; and the two lower rows of eight acanthus leaves, which Vignola makes 'of the same dimensions as the Corinthian'.

FROM THE IONIC it takes: the volutes, four of them, drawn by exactly the construction of the Ionic capital - Esquie sends the draughtsman back to the Ionic volute plate rather than giving a new one - and, standing between and behind them, the astragal and the egg-and-dart echinus of a complete Ionic capital. Ware puts it well: the Composite is 'the large Scrolls, Echinus, and Astragal of a complete Ionic Capital' set over the two lower rows of leaves and the caulicoli of the Corinthian.

WHERE VIGNOLA DEPARTS FROM BOTH, and this is the part that gets drawn wrong:
1. The four volutes are set DIAGONALLY, as in Scamozzi's Ionic and unlike Vignola's own Ionic, which is a frontal capital with cushions on the flanks. The Composite has no cushions. A Composite drawn with a bolster on the side is an error.
2. The Corinthian's small central helices are GONE, replaced by two flowers. Draw the helices and you have drawn a Corinthian with extra scrolls, which is the commonest single mistake.
3. Vignola changes the leaves from the olive of his own Corinthian plate to acanthus. Both rows.
4. The bell gains a fillet, an enriched bead and an enriched quarter-round - members the Corinthian bell does not have - specifically, Vignola says, to make the bell more prominent under the volutes.
5. The cornice has NO MODILLIONS. It is denticular, and the dentil is the large Composite dentil: 1/5 D high, 1/6 D wide, interdentil 1/12 D, 1/4 D on centres - half again the Ionic and Corinthian dentil, with only one dentil between the corner double dentil and the one over the axis, against two in the Ionic and Corinthian and three in the denticular Doric. Because there are no modillions, the dentils need not resolve to the column axes at all.
6. The architrave carries fewer and larger members than the Corinthian's three fascias and cymatium.

THE VOLUTE AND THE ABACUS TOGETHER ARE 16 PARTS. Vignola gives that number directly. The abacus is 6, so the volute zone is 10, and since the two lower rows of leaves are Corinthian at 12 parts each, 24 + 16 = 40 leaves 2 parts for the astragal and its fillet - which is what is encoded. The egg-and-dart echinus is NOT stacked above or below the volutes; it stands between them at the same height, which is why it is not a separate member in the capital assembly and why the assembly still sums to 42. Esquie's alternative account - the capital 'Corinthian as regards its lower half and Ionic as regards its upper half', which would put the leaves in 21 parts rather than 24 - is recorded here and not followed, because Vignola's own statement that the leaves are of Corinthian dimension is the more specific claim.

CONFIDENCE. The skeleton is high: it is the Corinthian's, and three sources say so. The capital is medium: the 42-part total and the 16-part volute-with-abacus are Vignola's, the internal split is reconstructed to satisfy them. The architrave and the corona and cymatium of the cornice are LOW: Regola plate XXVIII carries those figures as drawn annotations and no consulted transcription - the 1889 translation, Esquie, or Ware - reproduces them, all three saying only that the Composite repeats the Corinthian proportions with fewer and larger details and no brackets. The 27, 27 and 36-part totals are not in doubt; the mouldings inside them are. This is why the pack's overall confidence is medium where the Ionic and Corinthian are high, and it is the first thing to correct if a good facsimile of the plate becomes available.

PROJECTION DATUM. For the pedestal, base, shaft and capital assemblies, projection_parts is the HALF-WIDTH measured from the axis of the column; the naked of the shaft at its lower diameter is therefore 18 parts and the naked at its upper diameter 15 parts. For the architrave, frieze and cornice, projection_parts is measured from the NAKED OF THE FRIEZE, which stands 15 parts from the axis - Ware: 'the lower band of the Architrave is made to come in line with the upper face of the shaft.' The two conventions are the ones the sources themselves use and the schema anticipates both. Cross-check: Vignola gives the column base a projection of 7 parts from the side of the column (18+7 = 25) and the pedestal die a width of 2 modules 14 parts (half-width 25). The base sits exactly on the die. The arithmetic closes, which is how we know the datum is read right.
